stem: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide and water formed on complete combustion of 24 g of methane gas. (Atomic masses, C = 12 u, H = 1 u, O = 16 u)
solution:
The balanced chemical equation is,

\(\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)

\((12+4)\quad 2 \times (16 \times 2)\quad 12 + (16 \times 2)\quad 2 \times (2+16)\)

\(= 16\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 64\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 44\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 36\ \mathrm{g}\)

Hence, 16 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) on complete combustion will produce 44 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

\(\therefore\) 24 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4} = \dfrac{24}{16} \times 44 = 66\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

Similarly, 16 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) will produce 36 g of water.

24 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4} \equiv \dfrac{24}{16} \times 36 = 54\ \mathrm{g}\) water.

stem: How much CaO will be produced by decomposition of 5g \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) ?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed final line reads "= 2.8 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)", which contradicts its own question — the stem asks how much CaO is produced, and the line's own arithmetic (56/100 × 5 g) is the CaO fraction. As printed it asserts that decomposing 5 g of calcium carbonate yields 2.8 g of calcium carbonate. The species has been corrected to CaO above; the value 2.8 g is the book's and is correct.]

Calcium carbonate decomposes according to the balanced equation,

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

\(40 + 12 + 3 \times 16 \qquad 40 + 16 \qquad 12 + 2 \times 16\)

\(= 100\) parts \(\qquad = 56\) parts \(\qquad = 44\) parts

So, 100 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) produces 56 g of CaO

\(\therefore\) 5 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) will produce

\(= \dfrac{56\ \mathrm{g}}{100\ \mathrm{g}} \times 5\,\mathrm{g} = 2.8\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaO}\)

stem: How many litres of oxygen at STP are required to burn completely 2.2 g of propane, \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\) ?
solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of propane is,

\(\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

\(3 \times 12 + 8 \times 1 \qquad 5 \times 22.4\ \mathrm{L}\)

\((44\ \mathrm{g}) \qquad (112\ \mathrm{L})\)

(Where 1 mol of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L of volume)

Thus 44 g of propane requires 112 litres of oxygen for complete combustion

\(\therefore\) 2.2 g of propane will require

\(\dfrac{112}{44} \times 2.2 = 5.6\) litres of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP for complete combustion.

stem: A piece of zinc weighing 0.635 g when treated with excess of dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) liberated \(200\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of hydrogen at STP. Calculate the percentage purity of the zinc sample.
solution:
The relevant balanced chemical equation is,

\(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2}\)

It indicates that 22.4 L of hydrogen at STP \(= 65\ \mathrm{g}\) of Zn.

(where Atomic mass of Zn = 65 u)

\(\therefore\) 0.200 L of hydrogen at STP

\(= \dfrac{65\ \mathrm{g}}{22.4\ \mathrm{L}} \times 0.200\ \mathrm{L} = 0.58\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\therefore\) percentage purity of Zn \(= \dfrac{0.58}{0.635} \times 100 = 91.33\%\)

stem:
Urea \([(\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}]\) is prepared by reacting ammonia with carbon dioxide.

\(2\,\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

In one process, 637.2 g of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) are treated with 1142 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). (a) Which of the two reactants is the limiting reagent ? (b) Calculate the mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) formed. (c) How much excess reagent (in grams) is left at the end of the reaction ?
solution:
[Textbook note (not an error): the book sets the part labels (a) and (b) inline in the middle of a sentence, so the line prints as "...because it produces (a) smaller amount of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)) (b) The molar mass..." — the (a) stands where the article "a" belongs, there is an unmatched closing bracket, and part (b) starts mid-sentence. The layout has been restored above so the three parts read as parts; every number, quantity and conclusion is the book's own and is unchanged.]

(a) We carry out two separate calculations. First : If 637.2 g of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) reacts completely, calculate the number of moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\), that could be produced, by the following relation.

mass of \(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow\) moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 637.2\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{NH_3} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{NH_3}}{17.03\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{NH_3}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{2\ \text{mol } \mathrm{NH_3}}\)

\(= 18.71\) moles \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

Second : The relation from 1142 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\):

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

The number of moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) that could be produced if all the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) reacted :

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 1142\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}{44.01\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}\)

\(= 25.95\) mol \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

It follows, therefore, that \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) must be the limiting reagent because it produces a smaller amount of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\).

(b) The molar mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) is 60.06 g. We use this as a conversion factor to convert from moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) to grams of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\).

mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 18.71\ \text{mol}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \times \dfrac{60.06\ \mathrm{g}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{1\ \text{mol}}\)

\(\therefore = 1124\ \mathrm{g}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

(c) Starting with 18.71 moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\), we can determine the mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) that reacted using the mole ratio from the balanced equation and the molar mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

The conversion steps are

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) grams of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

So that,

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) reacted \(= 18.71\ \text{mol}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}} \times \dfrac{44.01\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}}{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}\)

\(= 823.4\ \mathrm{g}\)

The amount of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) remaining (in excess) is the difference between the initial amount (1142 g) and the amount reacted (823.4 g):

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) remaining \(= 1142\ \mathrm{g} - 823.4\ \mathrm{g} = 318.6\ \mathrm{g} \approx 319\ \mathrm{g}\)

stem: A solution is prepared by adding 2 g of a substance A to 18 g of water. Calculate the mass percent of the solute.
solution:
Mass percent of A \(= \dfrac{\text{Mass of A}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{g}}{2\ \mathrm{g}\ \text{of A} + 18\ \mathrm{g}\ \text{of water}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{g}}{20\ \mathrm{g}} \times 100 = 10\%\)

stem: Calculate the molarity of NaOH in the solution prepared by dissolving its 4 g in enough water to form 250 mL of the solution.
solution:
Since molarity (M) \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{\text{Mass of NaOH / Molar mass of NaOH}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{4\ \mathrm{g}\,/\,40\ \mathrm{g}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{0.1\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = 0.4\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{M}\)

Note that molarity of a solution depends upon temperature because volume of a solution is temperature dependent.

stem: The density of 3M solution of NaCl is \(1.25\ \mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}}\) Calculate molality of the solution.
solution:
Molarity \(= 3\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

Mass of NaCl in 1 L solution \(= 3 \times 58.5\)

\(\therefore = 175.5\ \mathrm{g}\)

Mass of 1L solution \(= 1000 \times 1.25 = 1250\ \mathrm{g}\)

\((\because\) density \(= 1.25\ \mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}})\)

Mass of water in solution \(= 1250 - 175.5\)

\(\therefore = 1074.5\ \mathrm{g}\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\)

\(= \dfrac{3\ \mathrm{mol}}{1.0745\ \mathrm{kg}} = 2.79\ \mathrm{m}\)
